title: Context Shifting
opening: When every answer looks like the tool you already know, change the setting around the same question. A different place, group or domain can reveal an option your current assumptions hide. That option is a candidate to check, not proof it will work here.

labels.example: Try the same question in a different setting
labels.question: Question in the school setting

example.question: How might every student get a turn with a limited set of workshop tools?
example.current: One team keeps the kit for a full week while other teams wait.
example.shifted: A public library lends scarce books to many readers: a reader reserves an item, returns it by a due date, and the next reader can borrow it.
example.visible: The access bottleneck may be the handoff and time per borrower, not just the number of kits.
example.candidate: Try reserving one kit for a class period and returning it to a shared check-in.
example.boundary: The reusable relation is a scarce item moving between people. A library does not settle school bell schedules, tool safety, or teacher supervision. Test a small candidate in the school setting; the comparison alone does not show that access improved.

prompts.practice: Use a question you are actually considering. Note the question and its current setting, a different place, group or domain, what that context makes visible, and one candidate to check back in the original setting. Include a difference or a small test that could disprove the transfer. Save a partial draft if you want; unknown parts can stay open.

source.quote: Context Shifting: change the place, people or domain through which you examine the question. Keep the new possibility beside the filter that had hidden it.
source.boundary: The manuscript places Context Shifting among several perception-disruption techniques. This module focuses on context shifting and does not treat novelty alone as transfer evidence.
